hints: Look at the central carbon in lactic acid in Fig. 4.1 and list the four groups attached to it.
walkthrough:
Spot the carbon with four different neighbours**
Look at the middle carbon in lactic acid, the one bonded to $\text{OH}$. It holds $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{COOH}$. That is four completely different groups, so this is a chiral centre. Pyruvic acid has $\text{C=O}$ there, so it cannot do this.
Final answer: Lactic acid contains a chiral carbon / centre bonded to four different groups, so it exists as non-superimposable mirror images.

hints: Identify the longest chain containing the $\text{COOH}$ carbon as C1 and number to give the $\text{OH}$ substituent the lowest number.
walkthrough:
Name it like any substituted carboxylic acid**
The $\text{COOH}$ carbon is always C1. You have a three carbon chain, so propanoic acid. The $\text{OH}$ group is on C2, so add 2-hydroxy. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ as 2-hydroxypropanoic acid.

hints: Recall that a hydrogen bond needs an $\text{H}$ attached to $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ or $\text{F}$ on one molecule and a lone pair on $\text{N}$, $\text{O}$ or $\text{F}$ on the other.
Think which atoms in lactic acid ($\text{OH}$, $\text{C=O}$, $\text{COOH}$) and in water ($\text{H-O-H}$) can provide the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ and the lone pair.
Remember how to show partial charges and the direction of the lone pair relative to the dashed H-bond.
walkthrough:
Choose a valid H-bonding site**
You can use any $\text{O-H}$ as donor and any $\text{O}$ lone pair as acceptor. The simplest is the carboxylic $\text{O-H}$ of lactic acid donating to the $\text{O}$ of water, or the water $\text{O-H}$ donating to the $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{O-H}$ oxygen of lactic acid. Pick one clear $\text{O} \cdots \text{H-O}$ contact.

Draw the dashed bond and label it**
Draw a water molecule $\text{H-O-H}$ close to lactic acid. Join the two molecules with a dashed or dotted line between $\text{O}$ on one molecule and $\text{H}$ on the other. Label this line hydrogen bond. It must be intermolecular, not inside one molecule.

Add dipoles and the lone pair correctly**
Because $\text{O}$ is more electronegative than $\text{H}$, show $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ on the atoms involved, for example $\text{O}^{\delta-}$---$\text{H}^{\delta+}$---$\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Then draw a lone pair on the acceptor $\text{O}$ pointing directly along the H-bond axis. That lone pair to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ attraction is the heart of the hydrogen bond.

Final answer: Draw $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ near an $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{C=O}$ group of lactic acid with a dashed bond labelled hydrogen bond between $\text{O}$ and $\text{H}$ on different molecules, e.g. $\text{O}^{\delta-}$---$\text{H}^{\delta+}$; show correct $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ sequence and a lone pair on $\text{O}$ in line with the H-bond.

hints: Recall that the $\text{C=C}$ pi electrons repel the electrons in $\text{Br-Br}$ to induce a dipole as the molecules approach.
Think about what the pi electrons attack and where the $\text{Br-Br}$ bonding electrons go, and what type of intermediate is left on carbon.
Consider how the remaining bromide ion then attacks the positive carbon to complete addition.
walkthrough:
Polarise bromine as propene approaches**
Picture the electron rich $\text{C=C}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ pushing away the electrons in $\text{Br-Br}$. The $\text{Br}$ nearest the double bond becomes $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ and the far one becomes $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. Draw $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with the $\delta+$ end closest to the $\text{C=C}$.

Make the first C-Br bond and release bromide**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=C}$ bond to the $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ bond onto the $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to give $\text{Br}^{-}$. This leaves a carbocation intermediate, essentially $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, with a positive charge on carbon and one $\text{Br}$ already attached.

Attack by bromide to finish addition**
Now the $\text{Br}^{-}$ has lone pairs and the intermediate has $\text{C}^{+}$. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to the $\text{C}^{+}$. That forms the second $\text{C-Br}$ bond and gives 1,2-dibromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$.

Final answer: Electrophilic addition: $\text{C=C}$ attacks $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ of polarised $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ ($\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ closest to $\text{C=C}$); $\text{Br-Br}$ electrons move to $\text{Br}^{-}$; forms bromonium / carbocation intermediate $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ (or $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2^{+}$); $\text{Br}^{-}$ donates lone pair to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$. Curly arrows, charges, dipoles and lone pair shown.

hints: Compare $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH}$ to see what change at the $\text{CH(OH)}$ group needs $[\text{O}]$ and what small molecule balances $\text{H}$ and $\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Treat it as secondary alcohol to ketone**
Lactic acid has a secondary alcohol $\text{CH(OH)}$ which oxidises to a ketone $\text{C=O}$ in pyruvic acid. Add one $[\text{O}]$ on the left and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the right to balance: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH} + [\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Recall how ethanal forms a cyanohydrin and what mixture provides $\text{HCN}$ in situ.
Think how a nitrile $\text{CN}$ group is hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid on heating with aqueous acid.
Consider how the 1,2-dibromopropane from propene can be converted to propane-1,2-diol by aqueous alkali.
Identify the strong oxidising agent that converts a secondary alcohol to a ketone and a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
Build lactic acid from ethanal via the cyanohydrin**
Ethanal $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ undergoes nucleophilic addition with hydrogen cyanide. In the lab you use $\text{HCN}$ with a trace of $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ (or $\text{KCN/NaCN}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$), cold, to give the cyanohydrin $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$. This adds the extra carbon needed for the acid group.

Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
Heat the cyanohydrin with dilute aqueous $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The $\text{CN}$ group hydrolyses to $\text{COOH}$, giving lactic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. This is the second step of Fig. 4.4.

Convert dibromopropane to the diol for the propene route**
In Fig. 4.3 the first step already gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br}$. Heat with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to substitute both $\text{Br}$ atoms by $\text{OH}$, forming propane-1,2-diol $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$. Aqueous conditions favour substitution over elimination.

Oxidise to pyruvic acid in the final step**
Both routes finish by oxidising lactic acid, or in the propene case the diol, to pyruvic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH}$. Use acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with heat. It oxidises the secondary alcohol to a ketone and, where present, the primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid.

Final answer: Synthesis from propene: second step $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, heat, to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$; third step acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, heat. Synthesis from ethanal: first step $\text{HCN}$ with $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, cold; second step dilute / aqueous $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat; third step acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, heat.
